**Lecture:** [Defining tables with PostgreSQL](week-03-defining-relations-with-sql.qmd).

These are syntax patterns to adapt, not a script to run in order. Replace names such as `table_name` and `column_name` with your own names.

## Create a table

```sql
CREATE TABLE table_name (
    column_name data_type,
    another_column data_type
);
```

Separate definitions with commas; do not put a comma after the last one. Add column rules after the type, and table-level rules as separate items inside the parentheses.

| Purpose | Definition inside `CREATE TABLE` |
|---|---|
| Generated primary key | `id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY` |
| Required value | `title text NOT NULL` |
| Required, unique value | `username text NOT NULL UNIQUE` |
| Default value | `is_available boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true` |
| Allowed range | `rating integer CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5)` |
| Allowed text values | `status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active', 'closed'))` |
| Nonblank text | `title text NOT NULL CHECK (btrim(title) <> '')` |
| Foreign key | `player_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES player_account(player_id)` |
| Unique combination | `UNIQUE (player_id, game_id)` |
| Named table-level check | `CONSTRAINT session_time_order CHECK (ended_at IS NULL OR ended_at > started_at)` |

For a foreign key, append a deletion policy after `REFERENCES other_table(id)`:

- `ON DELETE NO ACTION`: rejects a deletion that leaves a broken reference in our examples; this is the default.
- `ON DELETE CASCADE`: also deletes the rows that reference the deleted parent.
- `ON DELETE SET NULL`: clears the reference; the referencing column must allow `NULL`.

## Alter an existing table

Use `ALTER TABLE table_name` followed by one of these actions and a semicolon:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table_name
ADD COLUMN column_name text;
```

| Change | Action after `ALTER TABLE table_name` |
|---|---|
| Add a column | `ADD COLUMN column_name data_type` |
| Drop a column and its values | `DROP COLUMN column_name` |
| Add a named check | `ADD CONSTRAINT constraint_name CHECK (condition)` |
| Drop a named constraint | `DROP CONSTRAINT constraint_name` |
| Set a default | `ALTER COLUMN column_name SET DEFAULT value` |
| Remove a default | `ALTER COLUMN column_name DROP DEFAULT` |
| Require a value | `ALTER COLUMN column_name SET NOT NULL` |
| Allow missing values | `ALTER COLUMN column_name DROP NOT NULL` |
| Rename a column | `RENAME COLUMN old_name TO new_name` |
| Change a column's type | `ALTER COLUMN column_name TYPE new_type` |

**Remember:**

- A default supplies an omitted value; it does not reject an explicit `NULL`. Use `NOT NULL` when a value is required.
- A `CHECK` rejects false, so a check alone may allow `NULL`.
- New constraints and type changes must work with existing data. Some type changes need a `USING` expression.
- Changing a default does not rewrite existing rows. Dropping a constraint keeps the column's data; dropping a column removes it.
